arXiv:1011.3334v1 [math.AP] 15 Nov 2010

Positive solutions of some parabolic system with cross-diffusion and nonlocal initial conditions

Christoph Walker Email: walker@ifam.uni-hannover.de Address: Leibniz Universität Hannover, Institut für Angewandte Mathematik,
Welfengarten 1, D–30167 Hannover, Germany
Abstract

The paper is concerned with a system consisting of two coupled nonlinear parabolic equations with a cross-diffusion term, where the solutions at positive times define the initial states. The equations arise as steady state equations of an age-structured predator-prey system with spatial dispersion. Based on unilateral global bifurcation methods for Fredholm operators and on maximal regularity for parabolic equations, global bifurcation of positive solutions is derived.

Keywords:
cross-diffusion, age structure, global bifurcation, Fredholm operator, maximal regularity

1 Introduction

Consider the situation that an age-structured prey and an age-structured predator population inhabit the same spatial region Ω\Omega, that the individuals of both populations undergo spatial fluctuation and that the predator population exerts a repulsive pressure on the prey population. If u=u⁡(t,a,x)≥0u=u(t,a,x)\geq 0 and v=v⁡(t,a,x)≥0v=v(t,a,x)\geq 0 denote the density of the prey and the predator population, respectively, at time t≥0t\geq 0, age a∈[0,am)a\in[0,a_{m}) for a maximal age am>0a_{m}>0, and spatial position x∈Ωx\in\Omega, a simple model reads

∂tu+∂au−Δx​((δ1+γ​v)​u)\displaystyle\partial_{t}u+\partial_{a}u-\Delta_{x}\left(\left(\delta_{1}+\gamma v\right)u\right) =−α1​u2−α2​u​v,t>0,a∈(0,am),x∈Ω,\displaystyle=-\alpha_{1}u^{2}-\alpha_{2}uv\ ,\quad t>0\ ,\quad a\in(0,a_{m})\ ,\quad x\in\Omega\ , (1.1)
∂tv+∂av−δ2​Δx​v\displaystyle\partial_{t}v+\partial_{a}v-\delta_{2}\Delta_{x}v =−β1​v2+β2​v​u,t>0,a∈(0,am),x∈Ω.\displaystyle=-\beta_{1}v^{2}+\beta_{2}vu\ ,\quad t>0\ ,\quad a\in(0,a_{m})\ ,\quad x\in\Omega\ . (1.2)

These equations are subject to the nonlocal age boundary conditions

u⁡(t,0,x)\displaystyle u(t,0,x) =∫0amB1​(a)​u​(t,a,x)​𝑑a,t>0,x∈Ω,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{a_{m}}B_{1}(a)\,u(t,a,x)\,\mathrm{d}a\ ,\quad t>0\ ,\quad x\in\Omega\ , (1.3)
v⁡(t,0,x)\displaystyle v(t,0,x) =∫0amB2​(a)​v​(t,a,x)​𝑑a,t>0,x∈Ω,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{a_{m}}B_{2}(a)\,v(t,a,x)\,\mathrm{d}a\ ,\quad t>0\ ,\quad x\in\Omega\ , (1.4)

the spatial boundary conditions

u⁡(t,a,x)\displaystyle u(t,a,x) =0,t>0,a∈(0,am),x∈∂Ω,\displaystyle=0\ ,\quad t>0\ ,\quad a\in(0,a_{m})\ ,\quad x\in\partial\Omega\ , (1.5)
v⁡(t,a,x)\displaystyle v(t,a,x) =0,t>0,a∈(0,am),x∈∂Ω,\displaystyle=0\ ,\quad t>0\ ,\quad a\in(0,a_{m})\ ,\quad x\in\partial\Omega\ , (1.6)

and are supplemented with time initial conditions. The Δx\Delta_{x}-term in (1.1) describes spatial movement of prey individuals. Besides intrinsic dispersion with coefficient δ1>0\delta_{1}>0, it reflects an increase of the dispersive force on the prey by repulsive interference with an increase of the predator population. Here, γ≥0\gamma\geq 0 is the predator population pressure coefficient. We refer to [24] for a derivation of such kind of models (without age-structure). The right hand sides of (1.1) and (1.2) take into account intra- and inter-specific interactions of the two populations with positive coefficients α1,α2,β1,β2>0\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{1},\beta_{2}>0. Equations (1.5) and (1.6) describe creation of new individuals with nonnegative birth rates B1B_{1} and B2B_{2}. The reader is referred to [32] and the references therein for further information about linear and nonlinear age-structured population equations with (and without) spatial dispersal. Although such models have a long history, there does not seem to be much literature about equations with nonlinear diffusion. The well-posedness of equations (1.1)-(1.6) might be derived within the general framework presented in [28] though the results therein do not directly apply due to the cross-diffusion term.

We shall remark that the model considered herein is a rather simple biological model and there may be more accurate models, e.g. with different maximal ages, nonlocal dependences in the reaction terms etc. The aim of the present paper is thus rather to provide a mathematical framework to treat parabolic equations with cross-diffusion and nonlocal initial conditions. Namely, the present paper is dedicated to positive equilibrium (i.e. time-independent) solutions to (1.1)-(1.6) which shall be established based on global bifurcation methods. We write the birth rates in the form B1​(a)=η​b1​(a)B_{1}(a)=\eta b_{1}(a) and B2​(a)=ξ​b2​(a)B_{2}(a)=\xi b_{2}(a), where b1b_{1}, b2b_{2} are some fixed birth profiles and the parameters η\eta, ξ\xi measuring the intensities of the fertility shall serve as bifurcation parameters. Aiming at a simple and compact notation, we let b:=b1=b2b:=b_{1}=b_{2} and δ1=δ2=1\delta_{1}=\delta_{2}=1. We emphasize that these simplifications are made merely for the sake of readability and do not impact in any way on the mathematical analysis to follow. To shorten notation further, we shall agree upon the following convention: given a function defined on J:=[0,am]J:=[0,a_{m}] and denoted by a lower case letter, say uu or vv, we use the corresponding capital letter UU or VV to denote its age-integral with weight bb, i.e.,

U:=∫0amb⁡(a)​u​(a)​𝑑a,V:=∫0amb⁡(a)​v​(a)​𝑑a.U:=\int_{0}^{a_{m}}b(a)u(a)\,\mathrm{d}a\ ,\quad V:=\int_{0}^{a_{m}}b(a)v(a)\,\mathrm{d}a\ . (1.7)

Depending on the values of the parameters η\eta and ξ\xi, we are looking for nonnegative and nontrivial functions u=u⁡(a,x)u=u(a,x) and v=v⁡(a,x)v=v(a,x) satisfying the nonlinear parabolic system with cross-diffusion

∂au−Δx​((1+γ​v)​u)\displaystyle\partial_{a}u-\Delta_{x}\big((1+\gamma v)u\big) =−α1​u2−α2​u​v,a∈(0,am),x∈Ω,\displaystyle=-\alpha_{1}u^{2}-\alpha_{2}uv\ ,\quad a\in(0,a_{m})\ ,\quad x\in\Omega\ , (1.8)
∂av−Δx​v\displaystyle\partial_{a}v-\Delta_{x}v =−β1​v2+β2​v​u,a∈(0,am),x∈Ω,\displaystyle=-\beta_{1}v^{2}+\beta_{2}vu\ ,\,\quad a\in(0,a_{m})\ ,\quad x\in\Omega\ , (1.9)

subject to the nonlocal initial conditions

u⁡(0,x)\displaystyle u(0,x) =η​U,x∈Ω,\displaystyle=\eta U\ ,\quad x\in\Omega\ , (1.10)
v⁡(0,x)\displaystyle v(0,x) =ξ​V,x∈Ω,\displaystyle=\xi V\ ,\quad x\in\Omega\ , (1.11)

and spatial Dirichlet boundary conditions

u⁡(a,x)\displaystyle u(a,x) =0,a∈(0,am),x∈∂Ω,\displaystyle=0\ ,\quad a\in(0,a_{m})\ ,\quad x\in\partial\Omega\ , (1.12)
v⁡(a,x)\displaystyle v(a,x) =0,a∈(0,am),x∈∂Ω.\displaystyle=0\ ,\quad a\in(0,a_{m})\ ,\quad x\in\partial\Omega\ . (1.13)

Clearly, of particular interest are coexistence states, that is, solutions (u,v)(u,v) with both components uu and vv nontrivial and nonnegative.

Based on bifurcation techniques, existence of equilibrium solutions was established in [30, 31] for similar systems with linear diffusion and in [26, 27, 29] for a single equation with nonlinear diffusion. Except for [29], the bifurcation parameter was also chosen to be a measure for the intensity of the fertility as above. Prior to the just cited papers, bifurcation methods were used in [9] to derive positive equilibrium solutions for a single equations with linear diffusion. We also refer to [15] where the large time behavior of population dynamics with age-dependence and linear spatial diffusion was analyzed.

More attention attracted than the age-structured parabolic equations so far have related elliptic systems of the form

−Δx​[(1+γ​v)​u]=u⁡(μ−u±c​v),−Δx​v=v⁡(λ−v±b​u)-\Delta_{x}[(1+\gamma v)u]=u(\mu-u\pm cv)\ ,\quad-\Delta_{x}v=v(\lambda-v\pm bu)

in Ω\Omega subject to Dirichlet conditions on ∂Ω\partial\Omega with positive constants μ,λ,b,c\mu,\lambda,b,c; both for the case of linear diffusion γ=0\gamma=0 (e.g., see [3, 4, 8, 17, 18] and the references therein) and the case with cross-diffusion γ>0\gamma>0 (e.g., see [10, 11, 13, 14, 23] and the references therein). It is worthwhile to remark that for such elliptic equations with cross-diffusion, the transformation z:=(1+γ​v)​uz:=(1+\gamma v)u leads to a semilinear elliptic system for zz and vv, for which, when written in the form (z,v)=S⁡(z,v)(z,v)=S(z,v), the corresponding solution operator SS enjoys suitable compactness properties. Moreover, for such a system, positivity and a-priori bounds of solutions may be derived using the maximum principle, e.g. [10, 13, 23]. For the nonlocal parabolic equations (1.7)-(1.13) under consideration herein, however, a corresponding transformation still yields nonlinear second order terms with respect to the spatial variable (or first order time derivatives). Consequently, the underlying solution operator does not enjoy similar compactness properties. As we are interested in global bifurcation of positive solutions, it is thus not clear how to apply directly the unilateral global bifurcation methods of [16, 21] as in [30], which require compactness of the underlying solution operators. To overcome this deficiency, we shall invoke recent results of Shi &\& Wang [23] on unilateral global bifurcation for Fredholm operators, which are based on López-Gómez’s interpretation [16] of the global alternative of Rabinowitz [21] and on the global bifurcation results of Pejsachowicz &\& Rabier [19]. These results yield a (global) continuum of positive solutions. We shall also point out that, due to the cross-diffusion term, no comparison principle in the spirit of [30, Lem.3.2] is available. In some cases, the lack of such a comparison principle prevents us from determining which of the possible alternatives the constructed continuum of coexistence states satisfies (see Theorem 2.3 and Theorem 2.4 below).

2 Main Results

We suppose throughout this paper that the birth profile

b∈L∞+​((0,am))​with​b​(a)>0​for a near amb\in L_{\infty}^{+}((0,a_{m}))\ \text{with}\ b(a)>0\ \text{for $a$ near $a_{m}$} (2.1)

is normalized such that

∫0amb⁡(a)​e−λ1​a​𝑑a=1,\int_{0}^{a_{m}}b(a)e^{-\lambda_{1}a}\,\mathrm{d}a=1\ , (2.2)

where λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 denotes the principal eigenvalue of −Δx-\Delta_{x} on Ω\Omega subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Before stating our results on coexistence states in more detail, we first recall some auxiliary results from [30] about semi-trivial states, that is, about solutions (u,v)(u,v) with one vanishing component. Taking for instance v≡0v\equiv 0 in (1.8)-(1.9) and using convention (1.7), we obtain the reduced problem

∂au−Δx​u=−α1​u2,u⁡(0,⋅)=η​U,\partial_{a}u-\Delta_{x}u=-\alpha_{1}u^{2}\ ,\quad u(0,\cdot)=\eta U\ , (2.3)

subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. Introducing, for q∈(n+2,∞)q\in(n+2,\infty) fixed, the solution space

𝕎q:=Lq​((0,am),Wq,D2​(Ω))∩Wq1​((0,am),Lq​(Ω)),\mathbb{W}_{q}:=L_{q}((0,a_{m}),W_{q,D}^{2}(\Omega))\cap W_{q}^{1}((0,a_{m}),L_{q}(\Omega))\ ,

where

Wq,D2​(Ω):={u∈Wq2​(Ω);u=0​on​∂Ω},W_{q,D}^{2}(\Omega):=\{u\in W_{q}^{2}(\Omega)\,;\,u=0\,\text{on}\,\partial\Omega\}\ ,

and letting 𝕎q+\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+} denote its positive cone, the following result was proved in [30, Thm.2.1, Cor.3.3, Lem.3.6, Cor.3.7]:

Theorem 2.1.

Suppose (2.1) and (2.2). For each η>1\eta>1 there is a unique solution uη∈𝕎q+∖{0}u_{\eta}\in\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\} to equation (2.3). The mapping (η↦uη)(\eta\mapsto u_{\eta}) belongs to C∞​((1,∞),𝕎q)C^{\infty}((1,\infty),\mathbb{W}_{q}) and satisfies ‖uη‖𝕎q→0\|u_{\eta}\|_{\mathbb{W}_{q}}\rightarrow 0 as η→1\eta\rightarrow 1 and ‖uη‖𝕎q→∞\|u_{\eta}\|_{\mathbb{W}_{q}}\rightarrow\infty as η→∞\eta\rightarrow\infty. For η>1\eta>1 and a∈Ja\in J, the derivative ∂ηuη​(a)\partial_{\eta}u_{\eta}(a) is a (strictly) positive function on Ω\Omega. If η1>η2\eta_{1}>\eta_{2}, then uη1≥uη2u_{\eta_{1}}\geq u_{\eta_{2}}. Finally, if η≤1\eta\leq 1, then (2.3) has no solution in 𝕎q+∖{0}\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\}.

Given ξ>1\xi>1, we let vξ∈𝕎q+∖{0}v_{\xi}\in\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\} denote the unique solution to the corresponding equation for vv when taking u≡0u\equiv 0 in (1.8)-(1.9). Though we shall work in the solution space 𝕎q\mathbb{W}_{q}, we remark that solutions to (1.7)-(1.13), so in particular uηu_{\eta} and vξv_{\xi}, are smooth with respect to both a∈Ja\in J and x∈Ωx\in\Omega (see Lemma 3.7 below).

2.1 Bifurcation with Respect to the Parameter η\eta

We first shall keep ξ\xi fixed and regard η\eta as bifurcation parameter. We thus write (η,u,v)(\eta,u,v) for solutions to (1.7)-(1.13) with uu, vv belonging to 𝕎q+\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}. Theorem 2.1 entails, for any ξ≥0\xi\geq 0, the semi-trivial branch

𝔅1:={(η,uη,0);η>1}⊂ℝ+×(𝕎q+∖{0})×𝕎q+\mathfrak{B}_{1}:=\{(\eta,u_{\eta},0)\,;\,\eta>1\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{+}\times(\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+} (2.4)

of solutions. For ξ>1\xi>1, an additional semi-trivial branch

𝔅2:={(η,0,vξ);η≥0}⊂ℝ+×𝕎q+×(𝕎q+∖{0})\mathfrak{B}_{2}:=\{(\eta,0,v_{\xi})\,;\,\eta\geq 0\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\times(\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\})\ (2.5)

exists. In the latter case, a continuum of coexistence states bifurcates from 𝔅2\mathfrak{B}_{2}:

Theorem 2.2.

Suppose (2.1)-(2.2) and let ξ>1\xi>1. There exists η0:=η0​(ξ)>0\eta_{0}:=\eta_{0}(\xi)>0 such that an unbounded continuum ℭ\mathfrak{C} emanates from (η0,0,vξ)∈𝔅2(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi})\in\mathfrak{B}_{2}, and

ℭ∖{(η0,0,vξ)}⊂ℝ+×(𝕎q+∖{0})×(𝕎q+∖{0})\mathfrak{C}\setminus\{(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi})\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{+}\times(\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\})\times(\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\})

consists of coexistence states (η,u,v)(\eta,u,v) to (1.7)-(1.13). Near the bifurcation point (η0,0,vξ)(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi}), ℭ\mathfrak{C} is a continuous curve. There is no other bifurcation point on 𝔅2\mathfrak{B}_{2} or on 𝔅1\mathfrak{B}_{1} to positive coexistence states.

The value of η0​(ξ)\eta_{0}(\xi) corresponding to the bifurcation point is determined in (3.30).

We turn to the case ξ<1\xi<1, which is more involved. Recall that 𝔅1\mathfrak{B}_{1} is the only semi-trivial branch of solutions in this case.

Theorem 2.3.

Suppose (2.1)-(2.2). There is δ∈[0,1)\delta\in[0,1) with the property that, given ξ∈(δ,1)\xi\in(\delta,1), there exists η1:=η1​(ξ)>1\eta_{1}:=\eta_{1}(\xi)>1 such that a continuum 𝔖\mathfrak{S} emanates from (η1,uη1,0)∈𝔅1(\eta_{1},u_{\eta_{1}},0)\in\mathfrak{B}_{1}, and

𝔖∖{(η1,uη1,0)}⊂ℝ+×(𝕎q+∖{0})×(𝕎q+∖{0})\mathfrak{S}\setminus\{(\eta_{1},u_{\eta_{1}},0)\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{+}\times(\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\})\times(\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\})

consists of coexistence states (η,u,v)(\eta,u,v) of (1.7)-(1.13). The continuum 𝔖\mathfrak{S}

  • (i)

    is unbounded, or

  • (ii)

    connects (η1,uη1,0)(\eta_{1},u_{\eta_{1}},0) to a solution (η∗,u,v)(\eta_{*},u,v) of (1.7)-(1.13) with η∗∈(0,1)\eta_{*}\in(0,1) and u,v∈𝕎q+∖{0}u,v\in\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\}.

Near the bifurcation point (η1,uη1,0)(\eta_{1},u_{\eta_{1}},0), 𝔖\mathfrak{S} is a continuous curve. There is no other bifurcation point on 𝔅1\mathfrak{B}_{1} to positive coexistence states.

The values of δ\delta and η1​(ξ)\eta_{1}(\xi) are given in (4.5) and (4.6), respectively. Note that alternative (i) above always occurs if cross-diffusion is not taken into account, i.e. if γ=0\gamma=0, see [31, Thm.1.5]. Alternative (ii) stems from a technical condition, and we conjecture that alternative (i) is the generic case also for the present situation where γ>0\gamma>0. However, as occurrence of alternative (ii) is not ruled out by our analysis, Theorem 2.3 is rather a local bifurcation result in this regard.

2.2 Bifurcation with Respect to the Parameter ξ\xi

Since the cross-diffusion term involves the predator density vv, bifurcation from semi-trivial solution branches is more intricate when regarding ξ\xi (the measure of the predator fertility) as parameter and keeping η\eta fixed. We shall only consider the situation η>1\eta>1, the reason being explained in Remark 5.21. We now write (ξ,u,v)(\xi,u,v) for solutions to (1.7)-(1.13). Then, there are two semi-trivial branches of solutions

𝔗1:={(ξ,0,vξ);ξ>1},𝔗2:={(ξ,uη,0);ξ≥0}.\mathfrak{T}_{1}:=\{(\xi,0,v_{\xi})\,;\,\xi>1\}\ ,\qquad\mathfrak{T}_{2}:=\{(\xi,u_{\eta},0)\,;\,\xi\geq 0\}\ .

Also in this case, bifurcation from the semi-trivial branch 𝔗2\mathfrak{T}_{2} occurs:

Theorem 2.4.

Suppose (2.1)-(2.2) and let η>1\eta>1. There exists ξ0:=ξ0​(η)∈(0,1)\xi_{0}:=\xi_{0}(\eta)\in(0,1) such that a continuum ℜ\mathfrak{R} of solutions to (1.7)-(1.13) emanates from (ξ0,uη,0)∈𝔗2(\xi_{0},u_{\eta},0)\in\mathfrak{T}_{2} satisfying the alternatives

  • (i)

    ℜ∖{(ξ0,uη,0)}\mathfrak{R}\setminus\{(\xi_{0},u_{\eta},0)\} is unbounded in ℝ+×(𝕎q+∖{0})×(𝕎q+∖{0})\mathbb{R}^{+}\times(\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\})\times(\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\}), or

  • (ii)

    ℜ\mathfrak{R} connects 𝔗2\mathfrak{T}_{2} with 𝔗1\mathfrak{T}_{1}.

Except for the bifurcation point(s), ℜ\mathfrak{R} consists exclusively of coexistence states. Near the bifurcation point (ξ0,uη,0)(\xi_{0},u_{\eta},0), ℜ\mathfrak{R} is a continuous curve. There is no other bifurcation point on 𝔗2\mathfrak{T}_{2} or on 𝔗1\mathfrak{T}_{1} to positive coexistence states.

The values of ξ0​(η)\xi_{0}(\eta) and ξ1=ξ1​(η)>1\xi_{1}=\xi_{1}(\eta)>1, corresponding to the connection point (ξ1,0,vξ1)∈𝔗1(\xi_{1},0,v_{\xi_{1}})\in\mathfrak{T}_{1} if alternative (ii) occurs, are determined in (5.1) and (5.2), respectively. Given the assumptions of this theorem, if γ=0\gamma=0, one can show that alternative (ii) occurs if η\eta is less than a certain value or if additional assumptions on the birth rates and on αj\alpha_{j}, βj\beta_{j} are imposed, see [30, Thm.2.2].

The outline of the paper is as follows: The next section is dedicated to the proof of Theorem 2.2. In Subsection 3.1, we first introduce some notation, and in Subsection 3.2, we provide the necessary auxiliary results needed to perform the actual proof of Theorem 2.2 in Subsection 3.3. Sections 4 and 5 are dedicated to the proofs of Theorem 2.3 and Theorem 2.4, respectively. As these proofs are along the lines of the proof of Theorem 2.2, these sections are kept rather short.

3 Proof of Theorem 2.2

3.1 Notations and Preliminaries

Given two Banach spaces F1F_{1} and F0F_{0}, we shall use the notation ℒ⁡(F1,F0)\mathcal{L}(F_{1},F_{0}) for the set of bounded linear operators and 𝒦⁡(F1,F0)\mathcal{K}(F_{1},F_{0}) for the set of compact linear operators between F1F_{1} and F0F_{0}. We set ℒ⁡(F0):=ℒ⁡(F0,F0)\mathcal{L}(F_{0}):=\mathcal{L}(F_{0},F_{0}) and similarly 𝒦⁡(F0):=𝒦⁡(F0,F0)\mathcal{K}(F_{0}):=\mathcal{K}(F_{0},F_{0}). The set of toplinear isomorphisms between F1F_{1} and F0F_{0} is denoted by ℒ​i​s​(F1,F0)\mathcal{L}is(F_{1},F_{0}).

Let −ΔD-\Delta_{D} denote the negative Laplacian on Lq:=Lq​(Ω)L_{q}:=L_{q}(\Omega) subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions, that is, −ΔD:=−Δx-\Delta_{D}:=-\Delta_{x} with domain Wq,D2W_{q,D}^{2}, where

Wq,Dκ:=Wq,Dκ​(Ω):={u∈Wqκ;u=0​on​∂Ω}W_{q,D}^{\kappa}:=W_{q,D}^{\kappa}(\Omega):=\{u\in W_{q}^{\kappa}\,;\,u=0\ \text{on}\ \partial\Omega\}

for κ>1/q\kappa>1/q and Wq,Dκ:=Wqκ​(Ω)W_{q,D}^{\kappa}:=W_{q}^{\kappa}(\Omega) for 0≤κ<1/q0\leq\kappa<1/q. As q>n+2q>n+2, we have Wq,D2−2/q↪C1​(Ω¯)W_{q,D}^{2-2/q}\hookrightarrow C^{1}(\bar{\Omega}) by the Sobolev embedding theorem. In particular, int⁡(Wq,D2−2/q,+)≠∅\mathrm{int}(W_{q,D}^{2-2/q,+})\not=\emptyset, that is, the interior of the positive cone of Wq,D2−2/qW_{q,D}^{2-2/q} is not empty. Let γ0\gamma_{0} denote the trace operator defined by γ0​u:=u⁡(0)\gamma_{0}u:=u(0) for u∈𝕎qu\in\mathbb{W}_{q}, which is well-defined owing to the embedding [2, III.Thm.4.10.2]

𝕎q↪C⁡([0,am],Wq,D2−2/q).\mathbb{W}_{q}\hookrightarrow C\big([0,a_{m}],W_{q,D}^{2-2/q}\big)\ .

In fact, we have, due to the interpolation inequality [2, I.Thm.2.11.1],

𝕎q↪C1−1/q−ϑ​([0,am],Wq,D2​ϑ),0≤ϑ≤1−1/q.\mathbb{W}_{q}\hookrightarrow C^{1-1/q-\vartheta}([0,a_{m}],W_{q,D}^{2\vartheta})\ ,\quad 0\leq\vartheta\leq 1-1/q\ . (3.1)

In the following, we let 𝕎˙q+:=𝕎q+∖{0}\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}:=\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\setminus\{0\}. Recall that an operator A∈ℒ⁡(Wq,D2,Lq)A\in\mathcal{L}(W_{q,D}^{2},L_{q}) is said to have maximal LqL_{q}-regularity provided

(∂a+A,γ0)∈ℒis(𝕎q,𝕃q×Wq,D2−2/q),(\partial_{a}+A,\gamma_{0})\in\mathcal{L}is(\mathbb{W}_{q},\mathbb{L}_{q}\times W_{q,D}^{2-2/q})\ ,

where 𝕃q:=Lq​(J,Lq)\mathbb{L}_{q}:=L_{q}(J,L_{q}). Recall that −ΔD-\Delta_{D} has maximal LqL_{q}-regularity. If A:J→ℒ⁡(Wq,Dκ,Lq)A:J\rightarrow\mathcal{L}(W_{q,D}^{\kappa},L_{q}) for some κ≥0\kappa\geq 0, we write (A​u)​(a):=A​(a)​u​(a)(Au)(a):=A(a)u(a) for a∈Ja\in J and u:J→Wq,Dκu:J\rightarrow W_{q,D}^{\kappa}. The aim is to apply the global bifurcation results of [23, Thm.4.3,Thm.4.4] in order to establish Theorem 2.2. We first provide the necessary tools.

3.3 Proof of Theorem 2.2

Having established the necessary auxiliary results in the previous subsection, we are now in a position to prove Theorem 2.2 by applying [23, Thm.4.3,Thm.4.4]. Recall that, writing (η,u,v)=(η,u,vξ+w)(\eta,u,v)=(\eta,u,v_{\xi}+w), the solutions (η,u,v)(\eta,u,v) to (1.7)-(1.13) are obtained as the zeros (η,u,w)(\eta,u,w) of the smooth function FF defined in (3.11). Also recall that η0=η0​(ξ)\eta_{0}=\eta_{0}(\xi) is given in (3.30).

As in the second part of the proof of Lemma 3.13,

ker⁡(F(u,w)​(η0,0,0))∩rg⁡(F(u,w)​(η0,0,0))={0},\mathrm{ker}(F_{(u,w)}(\eta_{0},0,0))\cap\mathrm{rg}(F_{(u,w)}(\eta_{0},0,0))=\{0\}\ ,

whence

𝕏1=span⁡{(ϕ∗,ψ∗)}⊕rg⁡(F(u,w)​(η0,0,0))\mathbb{X}_{1}=\mathrm{span}\{(\phi_{*},\psi_{*})\}\oplus\mathrm{rg}(F_{(u,w)}(\eta_{0},0,0))

by [5, Lem.2.7.9] and Lemma 3.13. In view of Proposition 3.11 and Lemma 3.13 we may apply [23, Thm.4.3]. Therefore, there are ε>0\varepsilon>0 and continuous functions

η:(−ε,ε)→ℝ,(θ1,θ2):(−ε,ε)→rg⁡(F(u,w)​(η0,0,0))\eta:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\ ,\qquad(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}):(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\rightarrow\mathrm{rg}(F_{(u,w)}(\eta_{0},0,0))

with η⁡(0)=η0\eta(0)=\eta_{0} and (θ1,θ2)​(0)=(0,0)(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})(0)=(0,0) such that the solutions to (1.7)-(1.13) near (η0,0,vξ)(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi}) are exactly the semi-trivial ones (η~,0,vξ)(\tilde{\eta},0,v_{\xi}), η~≥0\tilde{\eta}\geq 0, and the ones lying on the curve Γ:=Γ+∪Γ−∪{(η0,0,vξ)}\Gamma:=\Gamma_{+}\cup\Gamma_{-}\cup\{(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi})\}, where

Γ±:={(η(s),sϕ∗+sθ1(s),vξ+sψ∗+sθ2(s)); 0<±s<ε}.\Gamma_{\pm}:=\big\{\big(\eta(s),s\phi_{*}+s\theta_{1}(s),v_{\xi}+s\psi_{*}+s\theta_{2}(s)\big)\,;\,0<\pm s<\varepsilon\big\}\ .

Moreover, Γ\Gamma is contained in ℭ∗\mathfrak{C}_{*}, which is a connected component of the closure of

𝒮:={(η,u,vξ+w);F⁡(η,u,w)=0,(u,w)≠(0,0)}.\mathcal{S}:=\{(\eta,u,v_{\xi}+w)\,;\,F(\eta,u,w)=0\,,\,(u,w)\not=(0,0)\}\ .

Being merely interested in positive solutions, we first note:

Lemma 3.14.

The curve Γ+\Gamma_{+} lies in ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}.

Proof.

Let us:=s​ϕ∗+s​θ1​(s)u^{s}:=s\phi_{*}+s\theta_{1}(s) and vs:=vξ+s​ψ∗+s​θ2​(s)v^{s}:=v_{\xi}+s\psi_{*}+s\theta_{2}(s). Then us​(0)=s​Φ0+o⁡(s)u^{s}(0)=s\Phi_{0}+o(s) and vs​(0)=ξ​Vξ+s​Ψ0+o⁡(s)v^{s}(0)=\xi V_{\xi}+s\Psi_{0}+o(s) in Wq,D2−2/qW_{q,D}^{2-2/q} as s→0+s\rightarrow 0^{+} by (3.1). Thus, it follows from Φ0,Vξ∈int⁡(Wq,D2−2/q,+)\Phi_{0},V_{\xi}\in\mathrm{int}(W_{q,D}^{2-2/q,+}) that us​(0),vs​(0)∈int⁡(Wq,D2−2/q,+)u^{s}(0),v^{s}(0)\in\mathrm{int}(W_{q,D}^{2-2/q,+}) for s∈(0,ε)s\in(0,\varepsilon) with ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough, whence us,vs∈𝕎˙q+u^{s},v^{s}\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} for s∈(0,ε)s\in(0,\varepsilon) due to the parabolic maximum principle [6, Thm.13.5] and (1.7)-(1.13). ∎

Now, invoking Corollary 3.8, Remark 3.9, and Corollary 3.12 we obtain from [23, Thm.4.4] (see also [23, Rem.4.2.1]) further information about the global character of the continuum. More precisely, if ℭ+\mathfrak{C}_{+} denotes the connected component of ℭ∗∖Γ−\mathfrak{C}_{*}\setminus\Gamma_{-} containing Γ+\Gamma_{+}, then ℭ+\mathfrak{C}_{+} satisfies the alternatives:

  • (i)

    ℭ+\mathfrak{C}_{+} intersects with the boundary of ℝ×𝕎q×𝕎^q\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{W}_{q}\times\hat{\mathbb{W}}_{q}, or

  • (ii)

    ℭ+\mathfrak{C}_{+} is unbounded in ℝ×𝕎q×𝕎^q\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{W}_{q}\times\hat{\mathbb{W}}_{q}, or

  • (iii)

    ℭ+\mathfrak{C}_{+} contains a point (η,0,vξ)(\eta,0,v_{\xi}) with η≠η0\eta\not=\eta_{0}, or

  • (iv)

    ℭ+\mathfrak{C}_{+} contains a point (η,u,vξ+w)(\eta,u,v_{\xi}+w) with (u,w)≠(0,0)(u,w)\not=(0,0) and (u,w)∈rg⁡(F(u,w)​(η0,0,0))(u,w)\in\mathrm{rg}(F_{(u,w)}(\eta_{0},0,0)).

Due to Lemma 3.14, the continuum ℭ:=ℭ+∩(ℝ+×𝕎q+×𝕎q+)\mathfrak{C}:=\mathfrak{C}_{+}\cap(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\times\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}) of solutions to (1.7)-(1.13) contains the curve Γ+\Gamma_{+}. Furthermore, we have:

Lemma 3.15.

ℭ∖{(η0,0,vξ)}⊂ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+\mathfrak{C}\setminus\{(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi})\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} is unbounded.

Proof.

We first show that ℭ+\mathfrak{C}_{+} does not reach the boundary of ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} at some point (η,u,v)≠(η0,0,vξ)(\eta,u,v)\not=(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi}). Suppose otherwise, i.e. let there be a sequence (ηj,uj,vj)(\eta_{j},u_{j},v_{j}) in ℭ∩(ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+)\mathfrak{C}\cap(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}) converging toward some point (η,u,v)≠(η0,0,vξ)(\eta,u,v)\not=(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi}) not belonging to ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}. Since uju_{j} and vjv_{j} are nonnegative, the limits uu and vv are as well. So u≡0u\equiv 0 or v≡0v\equiv 0 because (η,u,v)∉ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+(\eta,u,v)\notin\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}. We claim that neither is possible. Suppose first that both uu and vv identically vanish. As vj∈𝕎˙q+v_{j}\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}, ψj:=vj/‖vj‖𝕎q\psi_{j}:=v_{j}/\|v_{j}\|_{\mathbb{W}_{q}} is well-defined in 𝕎˙q+\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}, has norm 1, and

∂aψj−ΔD​ψj=−β1​vj​ψj+β2​ψj​uj,ψj​(0)=ξ​Ψj.\partial_{a}\psi_{j}-\Delta_{D}\psi_{j}=-\beta_{1}v_{j}\psi_{j}+\beta_{2}\psi_{j}u_{j}\ ,\quad\psi_{j}(0)=\xi\Psi_{j}\ .

The proof of Lemma 3.7 shows that (ψj)(\psi_{j}) is bounded in Cε​(J,C2+ε​(Ω¯))∩C1+ε​(J,Cε​(Ω¯))C^{\varepsilon}(J,C^{2+\varepsilon}(\bar{\Omega}))\cap C^{1+\varepsilon}(J,C^{\varepsilon}(\bar{\Omega})) for some ε>0\varepsilon>0 and so we may assume without loss of generality that (ψj)(\psi_{j}) converges in 𝕎˙q+\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} to some ψ\psi satisfying

∂aψ−ΔD​ψ=0,ψ⁡(0)=ξ​Ψ.\partial_{a}\psi-\Delta_{D}\psi=0\ ,\quad\psi(0)=\xi\Psi\ .

Thus ψ⁡(a)=ea​ΔD​ψ​(0)\psi(a)=e^{a\Delta_{D}}\psi(0), a∈Ja\in J, and ψ⁡(0)=ξ​H[0]​ψ​(0)\psi(0)=\xi H_{[0]}\psi(0) implying ξ​r​(H[0])=1\xi r(H_{[0]})=1 by the Krein-Rutman theorem. However, this contradicts (3.4) and ξ>1\xi>1. Next, assume uu vanishes identically but v≢0v\not\equiv 0. Then (η,u,v)=(η,0,v)(\eta,u,v)=(\eta,0,v) and the uniqueness statement of Theorem 2.1 implies v=vξv=v_{\xi}. Thus, (η,0,vξ)∈𝔅2(\eta,0,v_{\xi})\in\mathfrak{B}_{2} is a bifurcation point to positive coexistence states. By Lemma 3.7, we may assume (vj)(v_{j}) converges to vξv_{\xi} in Cε​(J,C2+ε​(Ω¯))∩C1+ε​(J,Cε​(Ω¯))C^{\varepsilon}(J,C^{2+\varepsilon}(\bar{\Omega}))\cap C^{1+\varepsilon}(J,C^{\varepsilon}(\bar{\Omega})) for some ε>0\varepsilon>0. Moreover, as above we may assume that (ϕj)(\phi_{j}), defined by ϕj:=uj/‖uj‖𝕎q\phi_{j}:=u_{j}/\|u_{j}\|_{\mathbb{W}_{q}}, converges in 𝕎˙q+\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} to some ϕ\phi satisfying

∂aϕ−ΔD​((1+γ​vξ)​ϕ)=−α2​ϕ​vξ,ϕ⁡(0)=η​Φ.\partial_{a}\phi-\Delta_{D}\big((1+\gamma v_{\xi})\phi\big)=-\alpha_{2}\phi v_{\xi}\ ,\quad\phi(0)=\eta\Phi\ . (3.33)

Therefore, ϕ⁡(a)=ΠAξ​(a,0)​ϕ​(0)\phi(a)=\Pi_{A_{\xi}}(a,0)\phi(0), a∈Ja\in J, and ϕ⁡(0)=η​Gξ​ϕ​(0)\phi(0)=\eta G_{\xi}\phi(0). Thus η=η0\eta=\eta_{0} by the Krein-Rutman theorem and (3.30). This yields the contradiction (η,u,v)=(η0,0,vξ)(\eta,u,v)=(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi}). Finally, suppose v≡0v\equiv 0 but u≢0u\not\equiv 0. Then we have (η,u,v)=(η,u,0)(\eta,u,v)=(\eta,u,0) what gives u=uηu=u_{\eta} with η>1\eta>1 by Theorem 2.1 since u∈𝕎˙q+u\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}, and so (η,u,v)=(η,uη,0)∈𝔅1(\eta,u,v)=(\eta,u_{\eta},0)\in\mathfrak{B}_{1} is a bifurcation point to positive coexistence states. As above we may assume that (ψj)(\psi_{j}), given by ψj:=vj/‖vj‖𝕎q\psi_{j}:=v_{j}/\|v_{j}\|_{\mathbb{W}_{q}}, converges to some ψ∈𝕎˙q+\psi\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} satisfying

∂aψ−ΔD​ψ=β2​ψ​uη,ψ⁡(0)=ξ​Ψ.\partial_{a}\psi-\Delta_{D}\psi=\beta_{2}\psi u_{\eta}\ ,\quad\psi(0)=\xi\Psi\ .

This readily implies 1=ξ​r​(H[−β2​uη])1=\xi r(H_{[-\beta_{2}u_{\eta}]}) what is impossible since ξ>1\xi>1 and 1=r⁡(H[0])<r⁡(H[−β2​uη])1=r(H_{[0]})<r(H_{[-\beta_{2}u_{\eta}]}) according to (3.4) and Lemma 3.6.

Consequently, ℭ+\mathfrak{C}_{+} intersects with the boundary of ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} only at (η0,0,vξ)(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi}), whence ℭ=ℭ+\mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{C}_{+}. So neither alternative (i) nor (iii) above is possible. Suppose (iv) occurs, and let (ϕ,ψ)∈𝕏1(\phi,\psi)\in\mathbb{X}_{1} and (η,u,vξ+w)∈ℭ+(\eta,u,v_{\xi}+w)\in\mathfrak{C}_{+} be with

(u,w)=F(u,w)​(η0,0,0)​[ϕ,ψ].(u,w)=F_{(u,w)}(\eta_{0},0,0)[\phi,\psi]\ .

Then ϕ−u=T1​(0,η0​Φ)\phi-u=T_{1}(0,\eta_{0}\Phi) by (3.27). Recall, from the definition of ϕ∗\phi_{*} and Lemma 3.13, that ϕ∗=T1​(0,η0​Φ∗)\phi_{*}=T_{1}(0,\eta_{0}\Phi_{*}) with Φ∗∈int⁡(Wq,D2−2/q,+)\Phi_{*}\in\mathrm{int}(W_{q,D}^{2-2/q,+}). The latter implies κ​η0​Φ∗+ϕ⁡(0)−u⁡(0)∈int⁡(Wq,D2−2/q,+)\kappa\eta_{0}\Phi_{*}+\phi(0)-u(0)\in\mathrm{int}(W_{q,D}^{2-2/q,+}) for some κ>0\kappa>0. Defining p:=κ​ϕ∗+ϕ−u∈𝕎qp:=\kappa\phi_{*}+\phi-u\in\mathbb{W}_{q}, we obtain p=T1​(0,η0​(κ​Φ∗+Φ))p=T_{1}(0,\eta_{0}(\kappa\Phi_{*}+\Phi)), that is, ∂ap+Aξ​p=0\partial_{a}p+A_{\xi}p=0 with p⁡(0)=η0​P+η0​Up(0)=\eta_{0}P+\eta_{0}U. Hence (1−η0​Gξ)​p​(0)=η0​U(1-\eta_{0}G_{\xi})p(0)=\eta_{0}U. Since u∈𝕎˙q+u\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} by assumption and thus U∈(Wq,D2−2/q,+)∖{0}U\in(W_{q,D}^{2-2/q,+})\setminus\{0\}, this last equation does not admit a positive solution p⁡(0)p(0) according to (3.30) and [1, Thm.3.2] in contradiction to p⁡(0)∈int⁡(Wq,D2−2/q,+)p(0)\in\mathrm{int}(W_{q,D}^{2-2/q,+}) by the choice of κ\kappa. So (iv) is impossible as well, and we conclude that ℭ∖{(η0,0,vξ)}⊂ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+\mathfrak{C}\setminus\{(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi})\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} is unbounded. ∎

To finish off the proof of Theorem 2.2 we merely have to remark that (η0,0,vξ)(\eta_{0},0,v_{\xi}) is the only bifurcation point.

Lemma 3.16.

There is no other bifurcation point on 𝔅2\mathfrak{B}_{2} or on 𝔅1\mathfrak{B}_{1} to positive coexistence states.

Proof.

Exactly the same arguments as in the first step of the proof of Lemma 3.15 show that there is neither a bifurcation point (η,uη,0)∈𝔅1(\eta,u_{\eta},0)\in\mathfrak{B}_{1} nor (η,0,vξ)∈𝔅2(\eta,0,v_{\xi})\in\mathfrak{B}_{2} to positive coexistence states. ∎

4 Proof of Theorem 2.3

As the proof of Theorem 2.3 is similar to the one of Theorem 2.2, we merely sketch it and point out the necessary modifications.

We shall derive a bifurcation from the branch 𝔅1\mathfrak{B}_{1} by linearizing around a point (η,uη,0)(\eta,u_{\eta},0) with a suitable η=η1\eta=\eta_{1} to be determined. First note that the smooth branch 𝔘:={(η,uη);η>1}\mathfrak{U}:=\{(\eta,u_{\eta});\eta>1\} in (1,∞)×𝕎˙q+(1,\infty)\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} of solutions to (2.3) provided by Theorem 2.1 extends to a smooth branch 𝔘∗:={(η,uη);η>η∗}\mathfrak{U}_{*}:=\{(\eta,u_{\eta});\eta>\eta_{*}\} in (η∗,∞)×𝕎q(\eta_{*},\infty)\times\mathbb{W}_{q} passing through (η,u)=(1,0)(\eta,u)=(1,0), where η∗∈(0,1)\eta_{*}\in(0,1) and −uη∈𝕎˙q+-u_{\eta}\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} for η∈(η∗,1)\eta\in(\eta_{*},1). Indeed, application of [26, Thm.2.4], [27, Prop.2.5] (with ε<0\varepsilon<0 in [27, Eq.(2.17)], see the proof of [30, Prop.3.4]) shows that the branch 𝔘\mathfrak{U} of positive solutions extends smoothly with a branch {(η(ε),uη⁡(ε));−ε0<ε≤0}\{(\eta(\varepsilon),u_{\eta(\varepsilon)});-\varepsilon_{0}<\varepsilon\leq 0\}, where −uη⁡(ε)∈𝕎˙q+-u_{\eta(\varepsilon)}\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} for ε∈(−ε0,0)\varepsilon\in(-\varepsilon_{0},0). Thus, fixing ε∈(−ε0,0)\varepsilon\in(-\varepsilon_{0},0), it follows that w:=−uη⁡(ε)∈𝕎˙q+w:=-u_{\eta(\varepsilon)}\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} satisfies

∂aw−ΔD​w=α1​w2,w⁡(0)=η⁡(ε)​W,\partial_{a}w-\Delta_{D}w=\alpha_{1}w^{2}\ ,\quad w(0)=\eta(\varepsilon)W\ ,

whence w⁡(0)=η⁡(ε)​H[−α1​w]​w​(0)w(0)=\eta(\varepsilon)H_{[-\alpha_{1}w]}w(0) and thus η⁡(ε)​r​(H[−α1​w])=1\eta(\varepsilon)r(H_{[-\alpha_{1}w]})=1 by the Krein-Rutman theorem. Due to Lemma 3.6 and (3.4), we have r⁡(H[−α1​w])>r⁡(H[0])=1r(H_{[-\alpha_{1}w]})>r(H_{[0]})=1 and so η⁡(ε)<1\eta(\varepsilon)<1. We thus get the desired smooth extension 𝔘∗\mathfrak{U}_{*} of 𝔘\mathfrak{U} by choosing η∗\eta_{*} sufficiently close to 11. Consequently, the solutions (η,u,v)=(η,uη−w,v)(\eta,u,v)=(\eta,u_{\eta}-w,v) to problem (1.7)-(1.13) can be obtained as the zeros (η,w,v)(\eta,w,v) of the smooth map ℱ:(η∗,∞)×𝕎q×𝕎^q→𝕎q×𝕎q\mathcal{F}:(\eta_{*},\infty)\times\mathbb{W}_{q}\times\hat{\mathbb{W}}_{q}\rightarrow\mathbb{W}_{q}\times\mathbb{W}_{q}, defined by

ℱ⁡(η,w,v):=(w−T⁡(−ΔD​(γ​v​(uη−w))−2​α1​uη​w+α1​w2+α2​(uη−w)​v,η​W)v−T⁡(−β1​v2+β2​v​(uη−w),ξ​V)),\mathcal{F}(\eta,w,v):=\left(\begin{matrix}w-T\big(-\Delta_{D}(\gamma v(u_{\eta}-w))-2\alpha_{1}u_{\eta}w+\alpha_{1}w^{2}+\alpha_{2}(u_{\eta}-w)v\,,\,\eta W\big)\\ v-T\big(-\beta_{1}v^{2}+\beta_{2}v(u_{\eta}-w)\,,\,\xi V\big)\end{matrix}\right)\ , (4.1)

and

Lemma 4.19.

5 Proof of Theorem 2.4

Again, the main part of the proof of Theorem 2.4 is a straightforward modification of Section 3, and we thus omit details. Let η>1\eta>1 be fixed. Linearization around (ξ,uη,0)∈𝔗2(\xi,u_{\eta},0)\in\mathfrak{T}_{2} entails the existence of a continuum ℜ+\mathfrak{R}^{+} in ℝ×𝕎q×𝕎q\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{W}_{q}\times\mathbb{W}_{q} of solutions to (1.7)-(1.13) bifurcating from (ξ0,uη,0)(\xi_{0},u_{\eta},0), where ξ0:=ξ0​(η)∈(0,1)\xi_{0}:=\xi_{0}(\eta)\in(0,1) is given by

ξ0:=1r⁡(H[−β2​uη]).\xi_{0}:=\frac{1}{r(H_{[-\beta_{2}u_{\eta}]})}\ . (5.1)

Near the bifurcation point (ξ0,uη,0)(\xi_{0},u_{\eta},0), ℜ+\mathfrak{R}^{+} is a continuous curve in ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} and it can be shown exactly as in Lemma 3.15 or Lemma 4.19 that ℜ:=ℜ+∩(ℝ+×𝕎q+×𝕎q+)\mathfrak{R}:=\mathfrak{R}^{+}\cap(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}\times\mathbb{W}_{q}^{+}) satisfies the alternatives:

  • (a)

    ℜ∖{(ξ0,uη,0)}\mathfrak{R}\setminus\{(\xi_{0},u_{\eta},0)\} is unbounded in ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}, or

  • (b)

    ℜ\mathfrak{R} reaches the boundary of ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} at some point (ξ,u,v)≠(ξ0,uη,0)(\xi,u,v)\not=(\xi_{0},u_{\eta},0) with u≡0u\equiv 0 or v≡0v\equiv 0.

If (b) occurs, choose a sequence (ξj,uj,vj)(\xi_{j},u_{j},v_{j}) in ℜ∩(ℝ+×𝕎˙q+×𝕎˙q+)\mathfrak{R}\cap(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}\times\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+}) converging toward (ξ,u,v)≠(ξ0,uη,0)(\xi,u,v)\not=(\xi_{0},u_{\eta},0). Putting ϕj:=uj/‖uj‖𝕎q\phi_{j}:=u_{j}/\|u_{j}\|_{\mathbb{W}_{q}} and ψj:=vj/‖vj‖𝕎q\psi_{j}:=v_{j}/\|v_{j}\|_{\mathbb{W}_{q}}, we may assume that ϕj→ϕ\phi_{j}\rightarrow\phi and ψj→ψ\psi_{j}\rightarrow\psi in 𝕎q\mathbb{W}_{q}. If both u≡0u\equiv 0 and v≡0v\equiv 0, then ϕ∈𝕎˙q+\phi\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} satisfies ∂aϕ−ΔD​ϕ=0\partial_{a}\phi-\Delta_{D}\phi=0 with ϕ⁡(0)=η​Φ\phi(0)=\eta\Phi and so 1=η​r​(H[0])1=\eta r(H_{[0]}) contradicting (3.4) and η>1\eta>1. If u≢0u\not\equiv 0 but v≡0v\equiv 0, then u=uηu=u_{\eta} according to Theorem 2.1, and ψ∈𝕎˙q+\psi\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} satisfies ∂aψ−ΔD​ψ=β2​uη​ψ\partial_{a}\psi-\Delta_{D}\psi=\beta_{2}u_{\eta}\psi with ψ⁡(0)=ξ​Ψ\psi(0)=\xi\Psi. Hence ξ=ξ0\xi=\xi_{0} by (5.1) what is impossible since (ξ,u,v)≠(ξ0,uη,0)(\xi,u,v)\not=(\xi_{0},u_{\eta},0). Therefore, the only possibility is u≡0u\equiv 0 but v≢0v\not\equiv 0. In this case necessarily ξ>1\xi>1 and v=vξv=v_{\xi} in view of Theorem 2.1. So ℜ\mathfrak{R} joins up with 𝔗1\mathfrak{T}_{1} at (ξ,0,vξ)(\xi,0,v_{\xi}). We remark that then the relation

η​r​(Gξ)=1\eta r(G_{\xi})=1 (5.2)

with GξG_{\xi} given in (3.29) must hold, since ϕ∈𝕎˙q+\phi\in\dot{\mathbb{W}}_{q}^{+} satisfies (3.33). That no other bifurcation point(s) on 𝔗2\mathfrak{T}_{2} or 𝔗1\mathfrak{T}_{1} exist(s) is immediate by the previous observations. This yields Theorem 2.4.

Remark 5.21.

Since the operator AξA_{\xi} in (3.28) does not yield a suitable maximum principle, there is no analogue of Lemma 3.6 for the spectral radius of GξG_{\xi} and the only information we have on r⁡(Gξ)r(G_{\xi}) is that it is positive for each ξ>1\xi>1 as observed in Section 3.2. Consequently, given η>0\eta>0, we cannot decide a priori whether (5.2) holds for some ξ>1\xi>1. However, for η>1\eta>1, if ℜ\mathfrak{R} joins up with 𝔗1\mathfrak{T}_{1}, then (5.2) must occur and the connection point (ξ,0,vξ)(\xi,0,v_{\xi}) on 𝔗1\mathfrak{T}_{1} is determined by this relation. Then again, the relation (5.2) is also a sufficient condition for the existence of a continuous curve of positive coexistence solutions bifurcating from 𝔗1\mathfrak{T}_{1}.

The same difficulty arises when considering bifurcation from 𝔗1\mathfrak{T}_{1} with respect to ξ\xi when η<1\eta<1 is fixed. In this case, (5.2) is again a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a bifurcation point on 𝔗1\mathfrak{T}_{1} to a curve of positive coexistence states, which then extends to an unbounded continuum.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
